# Solution

Let $w = z + i$. The series becomes $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{w^{n^2}}{n^3}$, with general term $a_n = \frac{w^{n^2}}{n^3}$.

We determine the set of $w \in \mathbb{C}$ for which this converges, then translate back via $z = w - i$.

## Case 1: $|w| < 1$ (absolute convergence)

Apply the root test:
$$|a_n|^{1/n} = \frac{|w|^{n^2/n}}{n^{3/n}} = \frac{|w|^n}{n^{3/n}}.$$
Since $n^{3/n} \to 1$ as $n \to \infty$ and $|w|^n \to 0$ (because $|w|<1$), we get $|a_n|^{1/n} \to 0 < 1$. By the root test, the series converges absolutely.

## Case 2: $|w| > 1$ (divergence)

Here $|a_n| = \frac{|w|^{n^2}}{n^3}$. Since $|w| > 1$, we have $|w|^{n^2} = e^{n^2 \ln|w|}$ growing exponentially in $n^2$, while $n^3$ grows only polynomially. Thus $|a_n| \to \infty$, so in particular $a_n \not\to 0$. The series diverges.

## Case 3: $|w| = 1$ (absolute convergence on the boundary)

When $|w| = 1$, we have $|w^{n^2}| = |w|^{n^2} = 1$ for every $n$. Therefore
$$|a_n| = \frac{|w^{n^2}|}{n^3} = \frac{1}{n^3}.$$
The series of absolute values is $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^3}$, which is a convergent $p$-series ($p = 3 > 1$). Hence the original series converges absolutely for every $w$ with $|w| = 1$.

## Conclusion

The series converges (absolutely) precisely when $|w| \leq 1$, and diverges when $|w| > 1$. Substituting back $w = z + i$, the condition $|w| \leq 1$ becomes $|z + i| \leq 1$.

The set of all complex numbers $z$ for which the series converges is the **closed disk of radius $1$ centered at $-i$**:
$$\boxed{\{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z + i| \leq 1\}}.$$
